title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 9: Jesus, Shepherd and Leader of All Time
keywords: Jesus Shepherd and Leader of All Time
Seek ye first the kingdom of God
Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone
the greatest of these is love
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Justice and Faith' -- CJP's BLD reflection on John 10:27-30 (the Good Shepherd discourse) delivered on the eve of the 1995 elections, presenting Jesus as 'the only leader truly worthy of emulation' and the standard by which newly-elected senators, congressmen, governors and mayors should be measured

Five leadership qualities of Jesus as the chapter's organizing structure -- (1) clear vision and mission; (2) courage and conviction; (3) servant-leadership; (4) prayer and faith; (5) justice and love -- each developed with scriptural anchors and a contrast to contemporary Filipino political practice

An unusual-leader opening framing -- Jesus's throne a wooden cross, crown of thorns, scepter a reed, ring a rusty nail; constituents who chanted 'Crucify Him' -- yet the only King who resurrected from the dead, conquering sin

A closing judge-pays-the-fine analogy that fuses justice and love -- the father-judge who imposes the speeding fine on his daughter, then pays it himself out of his wallet; the story of Jesus's atonement read as the cosmic instance of justice satisfied by love
sub_topics: Opening gospel -- John 10:27-30: 'My sheep hear my voice, I know them, they follow me, I give them eternal life'; continuation of the Good Shepherd discourse
Election context -- readings 'intended for last Sunday, one day before the election of our new government'; CJP applies the lessons to newly elected officials
Unusual-leader catalogue -- wooden cross, thorns crown, reed scepter, rusty-nail ring; constituents chanting 'Crucify Him'; resurrection as the king-mark

Quality 1 -- clear vision and mission: Sermon on the Mount as the 'greatest teaching of all time'; preference for the poor, the sorrowing, the simple-hearted, the peacemakers; opposition to hypocrite, arrogant, proud, self-righteous

Parables as pedagogy -- design to 'enable the listener to discover something for himself'; ending with questions ('Which of these three was neighbor...' Lk 10:36; 'Which of them was more grateful...' Lk 7:42; 'What fate do you suppose the owner...' Lk 20:16)

Quality 2 -- courage and conviction: Albert Nolan, 'Jesus Before Christianity' -- 'No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted'; mixing with sinners, tax collectors, the Samaritan woman, the prostitute, the adulteress
Mt 23:25-27 invective -- 'Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, you frauds!...you are like whitewashed tombs' -- Jesus naming opponents and denouncing sin without mincing words

Quality 3 -- servant-leadership: Mk 10:42-45 ('Anyone among you who aspires to greatness must serve the rest') contrasted with Filipino politicians who 'arrogate unto themselves power...allocate huge discretionary funds...dispense patronage and favors'
Foot-washing example -- Jn 13:14-16: 'I, who am Teacher and Lord, have washed your feet, then you, too, must wash each other's feet'

Quality 4 -- prayer and faith: Mt 14:23-24 (mountain retreat alone), Lk 22:44 (Gethsemane sweat 'like drops of blood'), 'Father, forgive them'/'into Your hands I commend my spirit' from the cross; the Lord's Prayer as the model

Quality 5 -- justice and love: Romans 14:17 (kingdom of God is justice, peace, joy); Mt 26:35-40 ('hungry...thirsty...naked...imprisoned'); Isaiah 42:1;6 ('he shall bring forth justice to the nations'); the adulteress (Jn 8:1-11) -- 'Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone'
1 Corinthians 13 -- 'If I speak with human and angelic tongues but do not have love, I am a noisy gong' -- love as the highest of three (faith, hope, love)
Judge-pays-daughter's-fine analogy -- the speeding-charge father-judge who removes his robe, walks to the court cashier, pulls out his wallet and pays the P500 fine; justice served and love satisfied
Atonement reading -- Jesus the judge who imposes the law of God on humanity for sin, then bears the guilt and pays the penalty Himself; 'such is the love of Jesus'

stances.claim: There is one standard of leadership and one leader truly worthy of emulation -- Jesus Christ -- and every elected official should be measured by His five qualities (vision, courage, servant-spirit, prayer, justice-and-love).
stances.rhetorical_move: ecumenical-yardstick: a Christological standard offered as the public-life measure for elected officials

stances.claim: Jesus's parables are pedagogically designed -- they end with questions to make the listener discover the truth -- a technique any teacher and leader can imitate.
stances.rhetorical_move: pedagogical-borrowing: parables read as a transferable teaching technique

stances.claim: True authority is service, not domination -- Filipino politicians 'arrogate unto themselves power...allocate huge discretionary funds...dispense patronage'; the contrast with Mark 10:42-45 makes the indictment specific.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-critique: scripture vs Philippine patronage politics

stances.claim: Justice and love are not opposed but converge -- the judge-pays-the-fine analogy shows justice satisfied and love expressed in one act; Jesus's atonement is the cosmic instance of this convergence.

stances.claim: Love is the highest theological virtue -- 1 Corinthians 13's catalogue of speech, prophecy, knowledge, faith, almsgiving and martyrdom all amount to nothing without love.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's BLD reflection on John 10:27-30 (the Good Shepherd discourse), delivered the night before the 1995 Philippine elections and offered to newly elected officials -- senators, congressmen, governors, mayors -- as the leadership measure. He opens with an unusual-leader catalogue (wooden cross, thorns crown, reed scepter, rusty-nail ring, 'Crucify Him' constituents) before naming the only King who resurrected from the dead, then expounds five leadership qualities of Jesus as the chapter's spine. First, clear vision and mission -- the Sermon on the Mount as 'the greatest teaching of all time,' preference for the poor and peacemakers, parables designed to make listeners 'discover something for themselves' (Lk 10:36, 7:42, 20:16). Second, courage and conviction -- Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity' on the courage to question tradition, sinners-and-tax-collectors company, the searing Mt 23:25-27 woes against Pharisees as 'whitewashed tombs.' Third, servant-leadership -- Mk 10:42-45 ('Anyone among you who aspires to greatness must serve the rest') is set against Filipino patronage politics in which leaders 'arrogate unto themselves power...allocate huge discretionary funds...dispense patronage and favors'; the foot-washing (Jn 13:14-16) is the example. Fourth, prayer and faith -- the mountain retreat (Mt 14:23-24), the Gethsemane sweat 'like drops of blood' (Lk 22:44), 'Father, forgive them' and 'into Your hands I commend my spirit' from the cross, the Lord's Prayer as the model. Fifth, justice and love -- Romans 14:17, Mt 26:35-40, Isaiah 42, the adulteress in Jn 8:1-11 ('Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone'), and St. Paul's hymn to love (1 Cor 13). He closes with a judge-pays-the-fine analogy -- the speeding lady-driver case in which the judge imposes a P500 fine then removes his robe, walks to the court cashier and pays it himself because the law-breaker is his daughter ('Justice was served -- and so was love') -- and reads the atonement as the cosmic instance of this convergence: Jesus the judge imposed the law of God for sin, then bore the guilt and paid the penalty Himself. 'Such is the Leader in Jesus. Such is the Shepherd that is Jesus. Such is the Shepherd of my soul.'
